title: The bow in the clouds (Genesis 8–9)
hook: after the flood, God's promise with every living thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Noah builds: a ship under a clear sky, and a man who did all things God commanded. Your line was build anyway. What plank did you lay? Day three hundred forty-three, the end of the week.

A hundred and fifty days, the water rules the earth. Then it begins to fall. The ark grounds on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven, which flies back and forth. Then a dove, which finds nowhere to land and comes back to his hand. He waits seven days and sends her again, and at evening she returns with an olive leaf in her beak. Seven days more, and she doesn't come back at all. A dove with an olive branch still turns up on flags and posters as a sign of peace. But the story isn't finished when the ground dries.
screen: `A RAVEN, BACK AND FORTH.` → `A DOVE WITH AN OLIVE LEAF.` → `THEN SHE DOESN'T COME BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, more than a contract, closer to a family bond. God promised one to Noah before the flood; here it is made. Second, who's in it. Not just Noah. God makes it with Noah, his sons, their children after them, and, the text keeps saying, every living creature: birds, cattle, beasts of the earth, everything that came out of the ark. The animals are named as partners in a promise. Third, what's promised: never again will a flood destroy the earth. And the sign. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth." The Hebrew word for bow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow. Some readers see a picture here: God hanging up the weapon, pointed away from the earth. That's an image readers have drawn, not something the text spells out. But the text is clear about who the sign is for: when the bow appears, God says, I will remember. The reminder is for God. Fourth, why the Church cares. The Catechism places this covenant with Noah within God's plan of salvation, and says it stays in force for the nations until the gospel is proclaimed to the whole world. And it closes a week that began with a lonely man in a garden, a serpent's question, a call into the trees, the first good news, a brother's blood, an ark, and now color across the sky.
screen: `BERIT: A BINDING PROMISE.` · `EVERY LIVING CREATURE IS IN IT.` · `A BOW HUNG IN THE CLOUDS.` · `THE REMINDER IS FOR GOD.` · then, large: `I WILL REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for color in the sky. If you can see a window, look out of it now. If not, picture the last sky you noticed. Settle, and breathe. Find whatever color is there: blue, gray, the orange edge of a cloud, the dull white of an overcast day. Let your eyes rest on it. Then think of every creature under that same sky right now: birds, a neighbor's dog, a stray cat, a fish you'll never see, a stranger across the world. All of them, in the story, inside one promise. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Covenant. Berit in Hebrew: a binding promise. After the flood, God makes one with Noah and every living creature, and sets a bow in the clouds as its sign.
Your line: a promise to every creature. Today, keep one small promise to an animal or a plant: fresh water, a walk, a little care. Day three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: The Church reads God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:8–15) on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, and the Catechism describes it as God's covenant with all the nations.

fork.setup: the waters have gone down and every creature is out of the ark. God speaks to Noah. what sign does God give?
options: a new altar built on Ararat.
a bow set in the clouds.
the dove that never came back.
fork.reveal: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant." and the reminder, the text says, is for God.

original.note: Hebrew: covenant, a binding promise. promised to Noah in Genesis 6 and made in chapter 9.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rainbow is a pretty ending to a sad story.
what it means: God binds himself in a promise to every living creature, and the bow reminds God to remember.
what a scholar hears: berit, covenant; qeshet, the word for a warrior's bow. the Catechism calls Noah's covenant the one with all the nations.

notes: Week end (days 337–343): the look-back sits at the end of the teach. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims Genesis 9:13 quoted from memory; confirm.
'First time in Genesis in full': berit first appears at 6:18 (promised to Noah) and is established in 9:9–17. Confirm the phrasing.
The bow as a warrior's bow hung up is an interpretive image; the script says so. Confirm.

The dove's flights (8:8–12): first returns with nothing, second with an olive leaf, third doesn't return. The raven 'went forth and did not return' in the Douay-Rheims (Vulgate) versus 'to and fro' in the Hebrew; the script says 'flies back and forth'. Confirm.
CCC 56–58 (covenant with Noah, in force while the nations last), CCC 71. Paraphrased; confirm. howItsDone: Genesis 9:8–15 is the first reading for Lent I, Year B; confirm.
